mappings.note: 'Why is she always unhappy' is answered by her refusal of her own station -- pride. Not LO-4: the item asks for the cause of the discontent, not a portrait.
The husband's character, plain. Not LO-17, which is Matilda's flaw; his contentment is the foil, not the fault.
She has no suitable dress. Extraction.
The four hundred francs. Extraction; why he gave them up is a separate item.
They borrow the necklace from Mme Forestier. Extraction.
How the replacement was funded and lived down. Extraction of the steps.
'The course of their life changed' is the ten years LO-17 names as the cost. Not LO-18: the falseness is not in question.
'The cause of Matilda's ruin', with how she could have avoided it, is the pride diagnosis outright.
A confession would have exposed the paste at once, so the item depends on the final revelation as well as on the pride that prevented it.
Asks the student whether they would have told the truth -- the pride-or-confession choice, transferred. Not LO-3: the demand is judgement, not length.
Francs, sous, Madame and M. as clues to a French setting. The chapter's setting item.
'Honesty is the best policy' asks for the writer's message as a maxim. Not LO-17, which is about pride rather than concealment.
Contentment as the lesson of the text. The writer's message, generalised.
Names Guy de Maupassant. Extraction; his technique is a separate outcome.
Dismissing the maid, changing lodgings, the husband's night work: the price of the pride, not incidental facts.
The letter about the jewel needing repair. Extraction of what was done.
The jewels were gone when she reached home. Extraction.
Elegant, gracious, full of joy. Extraction of the description.
Natural flowers instead of jewels. Extraction of his suggestion.
He grew pale. Extraction.
He expected her to be happy. Extraction.
Weeping for days after visiting her rich friend is the envy at the root of the pride. Not LO-1: the answer names the trigger of her discontent.
Shabby walls, worn chairs, poverty -- all three together are the discontent, not a list of furnishings.
What she believes she deserves is precisely the pride LO-17 names.
Five hundred francs is the revelation itself, stated as a number. Not LO-1, because the figure only matters against the thirty-six thousand.
Kitchen work, dishes, carrying out the refuse: the ten years in detail.
Thirty-six thousand francs. Extraction of the sum.
The loss of the necklace spoiled their pleasure. Extraction.
A necklace, against bracelet and Venetian cross -- the other pieces she refused. Extraction.
The gun. Extraction; the sacrifice it represents is asked in the short answers.
He was elated. Extraction.
A petty clerk. Extraction.
Dreaming of elegant dinners and marvellous dishes over her own plain table is the discontent at work. Not LO-1.
The Minister of Public Instruction. Extraction.
Meaning of 'stupefied'. No LO in this frame covers word-level vocabulary, so the competency is cited.
Meaning of 'dismay'. Vocabulary, so the competency.
The gun again, in a second MCQ. Extraction, treated as before.
Having no jewels. Extraction of the next obstacle.
Borrowing her friend's jewels. Extraction.
Danced, intoxicated with pleasure, thought of the admiration. Extraction.
The search, the police, the advertisement. Extraction.
His father's eighteen thousand plus borrowings. Extraction.
Ten years is the figure LO-17 turns on. Not LO-1: the number IS the cost of the pride.
'She told that hers were false' is the final revelation, as a single option.
A synonym-exclusion item on 'delicacies'. Vocabulary, so the competency.
The diamond necklace was missing. Extraction.
That it was worth no more than five hundred francs is the revelation. Same treatment as the other cost item.
Ten years to repay. The cost, again.
She had great success. Extraction.
That he underestimates her unhappiness identifies her discontent as the story's real subject. Not LO-4: the gap is hers, not his.
Maid gone, lodgings changed, an attic rented: the consequences of the debt.
Mme Forestier. Extraction.
Throwing the invitation aside because she has neither dress nor jewels is pride refusing a pleasure. Not LO-1: the key is 'both', i.e. the pattern.
Names the twist outright: the writer's withheld fact, and what the revelation means. Both outcomes, and not LO-17, which is the flaw rather than the ending.
Asks about the literary device itself and its impact on the narrative. The clearest LO-5 item in the chapter.
Contentment as the moral, argued from her downfall: the writer's message plus the pride that illustrates it.
Whether she accepted the hard life willingly, with reasons, is a judgement on the changed woman. Character, not LO-17, which is about the flaw that got her there.
M. Loisel as a loving husband, evidenced by the surrendered gun money. Character.
Fleeing the ball rather than be seen in a plain wrap, and what it shows about her -- pride, named by the item's second half.
Eighteen thousand of their own plus loans against the thirty-six thousand price. Extraction of the arithmetic.
Avoiding her rich friends because the comparison humiliates her. Pride, not a plot fact.
Their dismay on realising the loss. Extraction.
The lifestyle after the loss -- comforts surrendered, health broken. The ten years' cost.
The gun, and why he gave the money up. The second half makes it a character question rather than recall.
Four in the morning, before the glass. Extraction of how and when.

The broken-clasp letter is the device that keeps Mme Forestier from ever examining the necklace, which is how the decisive fact stays withheld to the last line. Not LO-1: the lie's function is what is being asked.
The invitation, and why it delighted him. Both stated. Extraction.
What happened at the ball, retrieved. The 'was her dream fulfilled' half is answered from the same passage.
The clerk's means and the household they could afford -- character and setting together, which is why the story's pressure exists.
The changes after the ball are the ten wretched years. LO-17.
'Trace the character arc' in 120 words: the woman across the story, the pride that moves her, and the long-answer form.
A diary entry on class and social mobility in M. Loisel's voice, which is the pride's cost seen from beside it. Not LO-18: the necklace's falseness is not the subject.
Written from Mme Forestier after the truth is out -- the revelation and what the reader is meant to feel, in her voice.
A dialogue whose opening line is the revelation itself. LO-18, extended into dialogue form.
A debate on frugality argues the story's lesson from both sides. Not LO-17: Matilda is the example, not the subject.
'Ostentation and vanity land people in trouble' with Matilda as the example is LO-17 named in the stem, at five marks.
An explicit character sketch of Matilda. Not LO-17, which would cover only the flaw.
An explicit character sketch of M. Loisel.
Why Jeanne cannot recognise her is the ten years written on her face. LO-17's cost, made visible.

Extract-based: retrieval about the borrowed jewels, plus her line that nothing is more humiliating than a shabby air among rich women, which is the pride. DEFECT of the known option-bleed kind: sub-question ii is printed inside option D instead of in the stem.
The extract is the meeting after ten years; sub-items ask why the days were hard and why she blames Jeanne, which needs both the cost and the coming revelation.

The sub-items turn on her deciding, now the debt is paid, to tell her friend everything -- the approach to the revelation. DEFECT: the extract itself did not survive extraction; the stem begins mid-sentence ('she had lived an ordinary life. to her?') and the answer key refers to material that is not printed.
